sentences.text: Duriavenator is estimated to have reached a length of 5 to 7 meters and a mass of one ton.
Its jaws held about four teeth in the premaxilla, 14 to 16 in the maxilla, and 14 to 15 in the lower jaw.
The bone process on the premaxilla was more prominent than in other basal tetanurans.
The maxilla features eleven foramina approximately 2 mm in diameter on the surface connecting with the premaxilla.
Two pneumatic chambers are visible in the corner of the antorbital fossa of the maxilla.
The dentary features tall, roughly pentagonal interdental plates on the inner side of the tooth row.
Two roughly oval Meckelian foramina are located in succession near the front end of the Meckelian groove in the dentary.
The preserved right dentary of the holotype contains parts of only the first 13 tooth sockets.
The genus name Duriavenator combines the Latin words for Dorset and hunter.
Researchers noted that the front teeth were longer than the back teeth, circular in cross-section, and inclined forwards.
A 2017 hypothesis suggested that lateral grooves on the dentary were sensory organs analogous to fish lateral lines.
Upper and lower jaw bones were collected near Sherborne in Dorset in 1882 by Edward Cleminshaw from the Inferior Oolite.
Richard Owen considered the fossils to belong to Megalosaurus bucklandii in 1883.
Michael Waldman prepared the specimen in 1964–1965 and designated it the holotype for Megalosaurus hesperis in 1974.
In 2008, Roger B. J. Benson redescribed the holotype, identified distinguishing features, and moved the species to the genus Duriavenator.
The species was originally classified under a different genus until it was moved to its own genus, Duriavenator, in 2008.
In 2016, Paul suggested that megalosaurids like Duriavenator were ambush predators that preyed on sauropods and stegosaurs.
Phylogenetic analyses from 2010 onwards show Duriavenator belongs to the family Megalosauridae and is among the oldest tetanuran theropods.
In 2008, researchers confirmed that Duriavenator belongs to the group Tetanurae.
The genus Duriavenator was established by Benson in 2008.
The species D. hesperis was originally described by Waldman in 1974.
Shared unique characteristics indicate Duriavenator was a member of the clade Tetanurae and specifically the family Megalosauridae.
According to Benson, Duriavenator is one of the oldest known species that certainly belongs to the Tetanurae.
A 2012 analysis by Matthew Carrano found Duriavenator to be a basal member of Megalosaurinae.
Duriavenator fossils date to the Bajocian stage.
Duriavenator lived during the Middle Jurassic, approximately between 171 and 167 million years ago, in the Bajocian stage.
During the Middle Jurassic, Britain was located in the subtropics and formed part of an island archipelago.
Duriavenator lived during the Bajocian stage, between 168.6 and 168.2 million years ago.
Waldman suggested Duriavenator may have had five premaxillary tooth sockets, which would make it unique among megalosauroids, though this number cannot be directly observed in the specimen.
The species name 'hesperis' refers to Hesperia, which British authors associated with Great Britain or West Dorset.
